lead: On the feast of the two great apostles the readings show the risen life of Christ working through weak human servants. In 2 Kings, the prophet Elisha prays over the dead son of the Shunammite woman, and the child opens his eyes. In Acts, Peter kneels and prays beside the body of Tabitha at Joppa and says, “Tabitha, get up,” and she rises: the power that worked through the prophets and through Jesus now works through his apostle. Paul, defending his ministry, lists his labours, prisons, beatings and shipwrecks, and boasts only of his weakness. And in John, the risen Lord asks Peter three times, “Do you love me?” and entrusts him with his flock, foretelling the death by which Peter would glorify God. Peter the shepherd and Paul the missionary both gave their lives in Rome. The Church also gives the readings of the Seventh Tuesday of the Apostles, which fit the feast well: love as the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:7–10), and Jesus healing in Peter’s own house (Mark 1:29–34).

set: Elisha succeeded Elijah as prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel in the ninth century before Christ. In Shunem, a village in the Jezreel valley, a wealthy woman had shown him hospitality and built a small upper room for him to stay in (4:8–10). She had no son, and her husband was old. Elisha promised her a son within the year.

The reading tells of the gift, the loss and the restoring of that child. The verses left out (22–31) tell how the mother rode to Elisha at Mount Carmel and would not leave him, and how Elisha’s servant Gehazi laid the prophet’s staff on the child without result. Elijah had raised a widow’s son in a similar way (1 Kings 17:17–24).
str: vv. 16–17: the promise of a son, and his birth “at that season”.
vv. 18–21: the boy falls ill in the harvest field and dies on his mother’s lap; she lays him on the prophet’s bed.
vv. 32–35: Elisha shuts the door, prays, and stretches himself on the child; the child sneezes seven times and opens his eyes.
vv. 36–37: “Take your son.” The mother bows and takes him.
kw: The usual title of Elisha in these stories. It means one who belongs to God and speaks and acts with his power.
Elisha does not raise the child by his own power. He first shuts the door and prays to the Lord. Every miracle in the Bible is God’s work.
Seven is the number of fullness. The child’s sneezing seven times is a sign of breath fully returned: life is the gift of God’s breath (Genesis 2:7).
vv: She went up and laid him on the bed of the man of God, closed the door on him, and left.
The mother says nothing to her husband of the death. She lays the child on the prophet’s bed, as if handing him back to the one through whom God gave him.
So he went in and closed the door on the two of them, and prayed to the Lord.
Prayer comes first. Jesus too put the mourners outside before raising Jairus’ daughter (Mark 5:40), and Peter will do the same at Joppa.
putting his mouth upon his mouth, his eyes upon his eyes, and his hands upon his hands
The prophet gives himself wholly, body to body, to the dead child. Some Fathers saw here a picture of the Son of God who came down to our measure to give us life.
She came and fell at his feet, bowing to the ground; then she took her son and left.
Her faith is rewarded. The story ends in silent thanksgiving.
ch: Several Fathers read Elisha’s action as a figure of the Incarnation: the Word made himself small, stretching himself, as it were, over dead humanity to give it life. The Church sees in the prophets’ miracles a preparation for Christ, who raised the dead by his own word, and for the apostles, who would act in his name. The Catechism distinguishes such raisings, which brought people back to ordinary earthly life, from Christ’s own Resurrection to a glorious life that can no longer die (CCC 646). Elisha’s miracle points ahead; Christ fulfils it.

set: After Saul’s conversion, the Church in Judea, Galilee and Samaria has peace (9:31). Peter is travelling among the communities, and at Lydda he has healed a paralysed man named Aeneas (9:32–35). Joppa, the port on the coast, the modern Jaffa beside Tel Aviv, was not far away. There a disciple named Tabitha has died.

Joppa is the town from which Jonah once fled from God’s call to the Gentiles (Jonah 1:3). In the next chapter, Peter, staying at Joppa, will receive the vision that sends him to the Gentile Cornelius (10:5–23).
str: vv. 36–37: Tabitha, a disciple rich in good works, dies; her body is laid in the upper room.
vv. 38–39: two men bring Peter; the widows weep and show the clothes she made.
v. 40: Peter sends all out, kneels, prays, and says, “Tabitha, get up”; she opens her eyes and sits up.
vv. 41–42: he presents her alive; many believe in the Lord.
kw: The feminine form of “disciple”, used only here in the New Testament. Tabitha is honoured as a true follower of Christ.
Tabitha is Aramaic, Dorcas Greek; both mean gazelle. Luke gives both names, as Joppa was a city of two languages.
The verb of resurrection. Peter’s words, “Tabitha, get up”, echo Jesus’ words to Jairus’ daughter, “Talitha cum” (Mark 5:41), which differ by one letter in Aramaic.
vv: She was devoted to good works and acts of charity.
Literally “full of good works and almsgiving”. Her holiness was in her needle and her generosity.
All the widows stood beside him, weeping and showing tunics and other clothing that Dorcas had made while she was with them.
The poor widows are her best witnesses. Each garment tells of her love. Charity is remembered long after we are gone.
Peter put all of them outside, and then he knelt down and prayed. He turned to the body and said, “Tabitha, get up.”
Peter does exactly what he had seen Jesus do in Jairus’ house (Mark 5:40–41). But he first kneels and prays: the power is not his own, but Christ’s.
This became known throughout Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.
The miracle is not an end in itself. It leads people to faith in the Lord.
ch: The Church sees in Peter’s ministry the continuation of Christ’s own: Jesus gave the Twelve a share in his power to heal and to raise (Matthew 10:8), and in Acts they act in his name, never in their own (Acts 3:12, 16). The Catechism teaches that the apostles were sent to continue Christ’s own mission, acting in his name and by his power (CCC 858–859). Tabitha, whose good works speak for her, is honoured in East and West as a model of practical charity, and many parish women’s groups in various lands have been named “Dorcas societies” after her.

r.h: I will boast of my weakness
set: In chapters 10–13 Paul answers rival preachers at Corinth who boasted of their Jewish descent, their eloquence and their visions. Paul hates boasting, but to protect the Corinthians he plays the “fool” and boasts for a while (11:1, 16–21). Yet he turns the boasting upside down: instead of successes, he lists sufferings.

His list matches what Acts tells: stoning at Lystra (Acts 14:19), beating with rods at Philippi (Acts 16:22–23), the escape from Damascus (Acts 9:23–25). It also tells of much that Acts does not record, such as three shipwrecks, all before the famous shipwreck at Malta, which came later (Acts 27). The forty lashes minus one was a synagogue discipline (Deuteronomy 25:3 allows forty; one was held back so as not to exceed the limit). That Paul accepted it five times shows he still counted himself a member of the synagogue and kept returning to his own people.
str: vv. 21b–23a: Hebrews, Israelites, descendants of Abraham, ministers of Christ: so am I, and more.
vv. 23b–27: the catalogue of labours, imprisonments, beatings, dangers and hardships.
vv. 28–29: daily anxiety for all the Churches; weak with the weak.
vv. 30–33: I will boast of my weakness; God knows I do not lie; let down in a basket at Damascus.
kw: A word Paul uses more than anyone else in the New Testament. For him the only true boast is in the Lord (10:17) and in the cross (Galatians 6:14).
His heaviest burden is not the beatings but the daily care for all the Churches. A shepherd’s heart suffers with every member.
The key word of these chapters. Paul will hear the Lord say, “power is made perfect in weakness” (12:9).
vv: Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I.
Paul never denies his Jewish identity. He remains proud to belong to the people of the covenant (Romans 9:3–5; 11:1).
Five times I have received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one.

These punishments were given by synagogue authorities in particular places, not by a whole people. Paul himself never blames his people as a whole; he prays for them with “great sorrow and unceasing anguish” (Romans 9:2).
And, besides other things, I am under daily pressure because of my anxiety for all the churches.
Here Paul speaks as a pastor. The care of souls is a heavier cross than any rod.
If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
The world boasts of strength; the apostle boasts of weakness, because there Christ’s power is seen.
but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall, and escaped from his hands.
An ironic ending. Roman soldiers were honoured for being first up an enemy wall; Paul’s “glory” is to have gone down a wall in a basket.
ch: St John Chrysostom loved Paul above all the saints and preached seven homilies in his praise; he marvels that this one man, weak in body, carried the care of the whole world in his heart (in substance, Homilies in Praise of St Paul). Pope Benedict XVI, in the Pauline Year 2008–2009, taught that Paul’s sufferings show that the apostle is united with Christ crucified, and that his strength came from Christ alone (in substance, General Audiences on St Paul). The Church honours Peter and Paul together because both gave their lives for Christ in Rome; St Clement of Rome, writing within a generation, already holds them up as examples of endurance (in substance, 1 Clement 5).

set: The risen Jesus has appeared to seven disciples by the Sea of Tiberias. After a night of catching nothing, they have hauled in a great catch at his word, and he has given them breakfast of bread and fish on a charcoal fire (21:1–14). The only other charcoal fire in the Gospels is the one in the high priest’s courtyard where Peter denied him three times (18:18). Now, beside a charcoal fire again, Jesus heals Peter’s threefold denial with a threefold question of love.
str: vv. 15–17: three times: “Simon son of John, do you love me?” Three times Peter answers, and three times Jesus entrusts his flock to him.
v. 18: the prophecy: when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will fasten a belt around you.
v. 19: the meaning: the death by which Peter would glorify God; then, “Follow me.”
kw: Jesus twice asks with agapaō; Peter answers with phileō, and the third time Jesus also uses phileō. Some Fathers and preachers have found a lesson here, but many scholars think John varies the words for style, since he uses both of the Father’s love for the Son (3:35; 5:20). Either way, the heart of the scene is the threefold question.
Two verbs: to feed and to shepherd, to guide and protect. Peter receives the whole care of the flock, lambs and sheep alike.
The flock remains Christ’s. Peter is a shepherd under the Good Shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep (10:11).
vv: Simon son of John, do you love me more than these?
Jesus calls him by his old name, as at the first call (1:42). Peter had once boasted that he would never fall away (Mark 14:29). Now he does not compare himself with the others.
Peter felt hurt because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” And he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.”
Peter no longer trusts his own word. He appeals to the Lord’s knowledge of his heart. Humility has replaced boasting.
But when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will fasten a belt around you and take you where you do not wish to go.
Early Christian writers understood this of crucifixion. Tradition holds that Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero, and Origen, as reported by Eusebius, says he asked to be crucified head downward.
After this he said to him, “Follow me.”
The last words of Jesus to Peter in John are the first words of every vocation. To shepherd is to follow, all the way to the Cross.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus entrusted a specific authority to Peter, and that after his Resurrection he confirmed it: “Feed my sheep” (CCC 553). The First Vatican Council and the Second Vatican Council cite this passage in teaching that the Lord made Peter the shepherd of the whole flock, and that this ministry continues in his successors, the bishops of Rome (Lumen Gentium 18, 22; CCC 881–882). St Augustine notes that the threefold confession answers the threefold denial, so that the tongue might show as much love as it had shown fear (in substance, Tractates on John 123). He adds that Peter is told to feed Christ’s sheep, not his own.

r.h: Love is the fulfilling of the law
set: These verses follow Paul’s teaching on the civil authorities. After saying “Pay to all what is due them,” he turns from debts that can be paid to the one debt that is never paid off: love.
str: v. 7: pay all their due: taxes, revenue, respect, honour.
v. 8: owe no one anything except love; the one who loves has fulfilled the law.
vv. 9–10: the commandments are summed up in “Love your neighbor as yourself”; love is the fulfilling of the law.
kw: Paul plays on the word: settle every debt, but keep this one always open. We can never say we have loved enough.
Love does not cancel the commandments; it fills them up and brings them to their goal.
vv: Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law.
A debt of love grows the more it is paid.
Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore, love is the fulfilling of the law.
Each commandment Paul lists protects the neighbour. Love does all that the commandments ask, and more.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it shows how Jesus and the apostle sum up the Decalogue in the twofold commandment of love (CCC 2055), and it teaches that charity is the soul of all the virtues (CCC 1827). On the feast of the two apostles, this is fitting: both Peter and Paul learned that love is the whole of the law, and both gave their lives for love of Christ.

set: This is the first day of Jesus’ ministry in Mark, a sabbath at Capernaum. He has taught in the synagogue and freed a man from an unclean spirit (1:21–28). Now he goes straight to the house of Simon and Andrew. Pilgrims from the fourth century onward venerated a house in Capernaum as Peter’s, and the remains of an early house church, later covered by an octagonal church, can be seen there today.
str: vv. 29–31: in Simon’s house Jesus raises up his mother-in-law, and she serves them.
vv. 32–34: at sunset the whole town brings the sick; he heals many and silences the demons.
kw: The verb Mark will use for the Resurrection (16:6). Jesus’ touch already brings the life of Easter.
From the word diakonia. The one who is healed becomes a servant, like the Son of Man who came to serve (10:45).
vv: Now Simon’s mother-in-law was in bed with a fever, and they told him about her at once.
Peter was married. The first healing in his house is for his family. The disciples bring a need to Jesus at once: this is the first form of intercession.
He came and took her by the hand and lifted her up. Then the fever left her, and she began to serve them.
Three gestures: he comes, he takes her hand, he lifts her up. Healing leads to service.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ’s compassion toward the sick and his many healings are a sign that God has visited his people, and that he wants to heal the whole person, body and soul (CCC 1503). St Jerome, preaching on this passage, prays that Jesus may come to our house too, take our hand and lift us up from the fever of our sins, so that we may rise and serve (in substance, Homilies on Mark).

qa: Why are Peter and Paul honoured on the same day?

Both were martyred in Rome under the emperor Nero, in the mid-60s, according to ancient tradition: Peter crucified, probably near the Vatican hill, and Paul beheaded on the road to Ostia. The Church in Rome has kept their common feast on 29 June at least since the fourth century. Together they stand for the two sides of the apostolic mission: Peter the shepherd and rock of unity, Paul the apostle to the nations. Very different men, sometimes in sharp disagreement (Galatians 2:11–14), they were one in faith and in love for Christ.
Did Peter really have authority over the other apostles?

The Gospels show Peter named first in every list of the Twelve (Matthew 10:2), given the name “Rock” (Matthew 16:18), asked to strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:32), and entrusted with Christ’s flock (John 21:15–17). In Acts he leads the first community (Acts 1:15; 2:14; 15:7). The Church teaches that this authority comes from Christ, and that it is a service of unity and love, continued in the bishop of Rome (CCC 881–882).
Why did Jesus ask Peter three times?

St Augustine and many others saw the threefold question as healing Peter’s threefold denial beside another charcoal fire (John 18:18). Each question gives Peter a chance to say with his lips the love that fear had silenced. And each answer is followed by a mission. Christ does not only forgive; he trusts again.
rite: In the East Syriac tradition, Peter and Paul are honoured within the Season of the Apostles, the season after Pentecost that celebrates the Church sent to the nations. The Syro-Malabar Church, which traces its faith to Mar Thoma Shleeha, rejoices in the communion of all the apostles: the faith Thomas brought to India is the same faith Peter and Paul sealed with their blood in Rome. Our Church lives in full communion with the successor of Peter, the bishop of Rome, and prays for him in the Holy Qurbana.

The reading from Acts is close to every parish: Tabitha’s needle and the widows’ tears speak of the many quiet works of charity in our homes and parishes. Like Peter, we kneel and pray first, then reach out a hand to lift others up.
study: Elisha and Peter both shut the door and prayed before acting. What place does quiet prayer have before I try to help others?
The widows showed Peter the clothes Tabitha had made. What will people show of my love when I am gone?
Paul boasts of his weakness, and his greatest burden is his care for all the Churches. How can I share that care through prayer and support for my parish and eparchy?
Jesus asked Peter, “Do you love me?” before saying, “Feed my sheep.” How does my love for Christ show in the way I care for those entrusted to me?
